questions.stem: On this chest radiograph, the inferior margins of several posterior ribs show scalloped erosions (highlighted). This finding is a classic sign of which condition?

explanation.summary: Rib notching results from dilated, tortuous intercostal collateral arteries eroding the undersurface of the ribs; it is a hallmark of longstanding aortic coarctation, in which blood bypasses the narrowed segment through the intercostal circulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rib notching results from dilated, tortuous intercostal collateral arteries eroding the undersurface of the ribs; it is a hallmark of longstanding aortic coarctation, in which blood bypasses the narrowed segment through the intercostal circulation.

questions.stem: This magnetic resonance angiogram of the thoracic aorta shows an abrupt focal narrowing (arrow) just distal to the origin of the great vessels. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: The discrete focal narrowing of the aorta near the isthmus (just beyond the left subclavian artery) on angiographic imaging is the defining feature of aortic coarctation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The discrete focal narrowing of the aorta near the isthmus (just beyond the left subclavian artery) on angiographic imaging is the defining feature of aortic coarctation.

questions.stem: These serial angiographic images of the aortic arch show a focal narrowed segment (black arrow), an inflated balloon at that segment, and a widened lumen afterward (white arrow). What procedure is being depicted?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Balloon angioplasty of an aortic coarctation

explanation.summary: The sequence shows a stenotic aortic segment, balloon dilation, and post-procedure luminal improvement, illustrating catheter-based balloon angioplasty used to treat coarctation of the aorta.

questions.stem: Compared with the normal heart (left), the right panel shows a thickened, incompletely opening valve between the right ventricle and pulmonary artery. Which chamber change would you most expect as a chronic consequence?

explanation.summary: Pulmonary valve stenosis increases the afterload on the right ventricle, which must generate higher pressures to eject blood through the narrowed valve, leading to concentric right ventricular hypertrophy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pulmonary valve stenosis increases the afterload on the right ventricle, which must generate higher pressures to eject blood through the narrowed valve, leading to concentric right ventricular hypertrophy.

questions.stem: The right panel shows a thickened valve at the outflow of the left ventricle that fails to open fully during systole. Chronic pressure overload from this lesion most directly produces which change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dilation of the aortic root aneurysm

explanation.summary: Aortic stenosis imposes a pressure (afterload) overload on the left ventricle, which responds with concentric hypertrophy (parallel sarcomere addition) to maintain wall stress while ejecting through the narrowed valve.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aortic stenosis imposes a pressure (afterload) overload on the left ventricle, which responds with concentric hypertrophy (parallel sarcomere addition) to maintain wall stress while ejecting through the narrowed valve.

questions.stem: These three schematics classify coarctation of the aorta by its position relative to the ductus arteriosus. The form that typically presents in the neonatal period with lower-body cyanosis and collapse when the ductus closes is which type?

explanation.summary: In preductal coarctation the narrowing lies proximal to the ductus arteriosus, so lower-body perfusion depends on right-to-left ductal flow; ductal closure after birth precipitates lower-body hypoperfusion and differential cyanosis, unlike the later-presenting postductal form.
explanation.whyCorrect: In preductal coarctation the narrowing lies proximal to the ductus arteriosus, so lower-body perfusion depends on right-to-left ductal flow; ductal closure after birth precipitates lower-body hypoperfusion and differential cyanosis, unlike the later-presenting postductal form.

questions.stem: The right diagram shows a focal narrowing of the aorta just past the origin of the left subclavian artery. In an adult with this lesion, which physical exam finding is classically expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Equal, bounding pulses in all four limbs

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cyanosis of the upper body only

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypertension in the legs with weak arm pulses

choices.label: D
choices.text: Continuous machinery murmur with wide pulse pressure

choices.label: E
choices.text: Upper extremity hypertension with diminished femoral pulses

explanation.summary: Coarctation distal to the left subclavian raises blood pressure proximally (arms) while reducing perfusion pressure distally, producing upper-limb hypertension and weak, delayed lower-extremity (radiofemoral delay) pulses.
explanation.whyCorrect: Coarctation distal to the left subclavian raises blood pressure proximally (arms) while reducing perfusion pressure distally, producing upper-limb hypertension and weak, delayed lower-extremity (radiofemoral delay) pulses.

questions.stem: This diagram traces blood flow around an aortic narrowing through the subclavian, internal thoracic, and intercostal arteries. This collateral pathway explains which radiographic finding?

explanation.summary: To bypass the coarctation, blood is shunted retrograde through enlarged intercostal arteries fed by the internal thoracic and subclavian vessels; the dilated, pulsatile intercostals erode the undersurface of the ribs, producing rib notching.
explanation.whyCorrect: To bypass the coarctation, blood is shunted retrograde through enlarged intercostal arteries fed by the internal thoracic and subclavian vessels; the dilated, pulsatile intercostals erode the undersurface of the ribs, producing rib notching.
